newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Nobel laureate invited to gathering for Suharto.
newsitem.headline: Nobel laureate invited to gathering for Suharto.

text.p: The bishop who shared the Nobel Peace Prize for his crusade against Indonesia's military presence in East Timor said on Monday he had been invited to a gathering for President Suharto during his visit to the territory on Tuesday.
"The local government has invited me. I will attend," Bishop Carlos Belo told Reuters from the East Timor capital, Dili.
Suharto is due to make a brief visit to inaugurate several projects in the former Portuguese territory invaded by Indonesia in 1975 and annexed the following year.

A gathering has been arranged for Suharto to meet local dignitaries at the office of East Timor's governor, Abilio Soares. Soares congratulated the bishop for receiving the award on behalf of the government on Saturday.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee on Friday awarded the 1996 peace prize jointly to Belo and self-exiled East Timor independence leader Jose Ramos-Horta, who lives in Australia.
Asked if he would meet Suharto face-to-face during the gathering, Belo said: "I don't know yet." He did not say whether he had met Suharto during two previous visits by the president.

One of the projects to be inaugurated by Suharto is a 27-metre (88-foot) statue of Jesus Christ with outstretched arms on a headland outside Dili -- believed to be the largest outside Rio de Janeiro. The government and the national airline Garuda Indonesia financed the construction of the 33-tonne statue.
"For Indonesians, the opening ceremony is important. But for us Catholics, more important is the blessing," Belo said, adding that the church had not been consulted over the statue.
The joint Nobel award caught the country by surprise, and many Indonesians have expressed anger at the naming of Ramos-Horta, described by Foreign Minister Ali Alatas as a "political adventurer".
But there has been general acceptance of Belo, a fiery Jesuit who is regarded as possibly the most influential man in largely-Catholic East Timor and a champion of East Timorese rights.

He has intervened to prevent violence in a territory where the military has brutally suppressed dissent on past occasions. Troops killed at least 50 protesters following a funeral march in 1991, according to official count.
Witnesses say up to 200 may have died.
The United Nations has refused to acknowledge Indonesian sovereignty over the territory of about 800,000 people and still regards former colonial ruler Portugal as the administering power.

Asked how he would use his half of the $1 million prize, Belo said he planned to fund a peace commission set up two years ago, the construction of a seminary to train priests and a scholarship fund for East Timorese students at Dili's university. He said some of the money also would go toward helping the poor.
He said he had not yet decided whether he would go to Oslo to accept the award in person.
